{{Short description|On graph coloring and neighborhood size}}
[[File:Graph exact coloring.svg|179px|thumb|[[Complete graph]]s need one more color than their maximum degree. They and the odd cycles are the only exceptions to Brooks' theorem.]]
In [[graph theory]], '''Brooks' theorem''' states a relationship between the maximum [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] of a graph and its [[chromatic number]]. According to the theorem, in a connected graph in which every vertex has at most Δ neighbors, the vertices can be [[graph coloring|colored]] with only Δ colors, except for two cases, [[complete graph]]s and [[cycle graph]]s of odd length, which require Δ&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 colors.

The theorem is named after [[R. Leonard Brooks]], who published a proof of it in 1941.{{sfnp|Brooks|1941}} A coloring with the number of colors described by Brooks' theorem is sometimes called a ''Brooks coloring''{{sfnp|Hajnal|Szemerédi|1990}} or a Δ-''coloring''.{{sfnp|Panconesi|Srinivasan|1995}}

==Formal statement==
For any [[connected graph|connected]] [[undirected graph]] ''G'' with maximum [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] Δ,
the [[chromatic number]] of ''G'' is at most Δ, unless ''G'' is a complete graph or an odd cycle, in which case the chromatic number is&nbsp;Δ&nbsp;+&nbsp;1.{{sfnp|Brooks|1941}}

==Proof==
[[László Lovász]] gives a simplified proof of Brooks' theorem. If the graph is not [[biconnected graph|biconnected]], its biconnected components may be colored separately and then the colorings combined. If the graph has a vertex ''v'' with degree less than Δ, then a [[greedy coloring]] algorithm that colors vertices farther from ''v'' before closer ones uses at most Δ colors. This is because at the time that each vertex other than ''v'' is colored, at least one of its neighbors (the one on a shortest path to ''v'') is uncolored, so it has fewer than Δ colored neighbors and has a free color. When the algorithm reaches ''v'', its small number of neighbors allows it to be colored. Therefore, the most difficult case of the proof concerns biconnected Δ-[[regular graph|regular]] graphs with Δ&nbsp;≥&nbsp;3. In this case, Lovász shows that one can find a [[spanning tree]] such that two nonadjacent neighbors ''u'' and ''w'' of the root ''v'' are leaves in the tree. A greedy coloring starting from ''u'' and ''w'' and processing the remaining vertices of the spanning tree in bottom-up order, ending at ''v'', uses at most Δ colors. For, when every vertex other than ''v'' is colored, it has an uncolored parent, so its already-colored neighbors cannot use up all the free colors, while at ''v'' the two neighbors ''u'' and ''w'' have equal colors so again a free color remains for ''v'' itself.{{sfnp|Lovász|1975}}

==Extensions==
A more general version of the theorem applies to [[list coloring]]: given any connected undirected graph with maximum degree Δ that is neither a [[clique (graph theory)|clique]] nor an odd cycle, and a list of Δ colors for each vertex, it is possible to choose a color for each vertex from its list so that no two adjacent vertices have the same color. In other words, the list chromatic number of a connected undirected graph G never exceeds Δ, unless G is a clique or an odd cycle.{{sfnp|Vizing|1976}}

For certain graphs, even fewer than Δ colors may be needed. Δ&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 colors suffice if and only if the given graph has no Δ-clique, ''provided'' Δ is large enough.{{sfnp|Reed|1999}} For [[triangle-free graph]]s, or more generally graphs in which the [[neighborhood (graph theory)|neighborhood]] of every vertex is sufficiently [[sparse graph|sparse]], O(Δ/log&nbsp;Δ) colors suffice.<ref>{{harvtxt|Alon|Krivelevich|Sudakov|1999}}.</ref>

The degree of a graph also appears in upper bounds for other types of coloring; for [[edge coloring]], the result that the chromatic index is at most Δ&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 is [[Vizing's theorem]]. An extension of Brooks' theorem to [[total coloring]], stating that the total chromatic number is at most Δ&nbsp;+&nbsp;2, has been conjectured by [[Mehdi Behzad]] and Vizing. The Hajnal–Szemerédi theorem on [[equitable coloring]] states that any graph has a (Δ&nbsp;+&nbsp;1)-coloring in which the sizes of any two color classes differ by at most one.

==Algorithms==
A Δ-coloring, or even a Δ-list-coloring, of a degree-Δ graph may be found in linear time.<ref>{{harvtxt|Skulrattanakulchai|2006}}.</ref> Efficient algorithms are also known for finding Brooks colorings in parallel and distributed models of computation.<ref>{{harvtxt|Karloff|1989}}; {{harvtxt|Hajnal|Szemerédi|1990}}; {{harvtxt|Panconesi|Srinivasan|1995}}; {{harvtxt|Grable|Panconesi|2000}}.</ref>
